hints: Focus on the p-subshell only, and remember Hund's rule that electrons stay unpaired in separate p orbitals where possible.
Write the p-electron count for pair 1: O is $2p^4$ and $Cl^+$ is $3p^4$, so both have the same p arrangement.
Now count p electrons for the ions in pairs 2 and 3, $F^+$ and $Ga^-$ both end as $p^4$ and $p^2$, while N and $Kr^{3+}$ both end as $p^3$, then check which pairs match.
walkthrough:
**Recall how to count unpaired p electrons**

Think of a p subshell as three boxes. One electron goes in each box first, then they start to pair up.

So $p^1$ has 1 unpaired, $p^2$ has 2 unpaired, $p^3$ has 3 unpaired, $p^4$ has 2 unpaired, $p^5$ has 1 unpaired, $p^6$ has 0.

**Check pair 1: O and $Cl^+$**

O (Z = 8) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$. That is 2 unpaired in p.

$$\text{O}: [He]2s^2 2p^4 \rightarrow \text{2 unpaired}$$

**Finish pair 1 with $Cl^+$**

Cl (Z = 17) is $[Ne]3s^2 3p^5$. Removing one electron to make $Cl^+$ removes a p electron.

$$\text{Cl}^+: [Ne]3s^2 3p^4 \rightarrow \text{2 unpaired}$$
So pair 1 matches, both have 2.

**Check pair 2: $F^+$ and $Ga^-$**

F (Z = 9) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^5$, so $F^+$ is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$ with 2 unpaired.

Ga (Z = 31) is $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^1$, so $Ga^-$ adds one p electron to give $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^2$ with 2 unpaired.

$$\text{F}^+: 2p^4 \rightarrow 2 \text{ unpaired, } Ga^-: 4p^2 \rightarrow 2 \text{ unpaired}$$
So pair 2 matches.

**Check pair 3: N and $Kr^{3+}$**

N (Z = 7) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$ with 3 unpaired, the half-filled stable arrangement.

Kr (Z = 36) is $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^6$. Removing three electrons gives $[Ar]3d^{10}4s^2 4p^3$.

$$\text{N}: 2p^3 \rightarrow 3 \text{ unpaired, } Kr^{3+}: 4p^3 \rightarrow 3 \text{ unpaired}$$
So pair 3 matches. All three pairs are correct.

options.A: Correct, because 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Pair 1 is $p^4$ and $p^4$ (2 unpaired each), pair 2 is $p^4$ and $p^2$ (2 unpaired each), pair 3 is $p^3$ and $p^3$ (3 unpaired each).
options.B: Incorrect. This would mean only 1 and 2 are correct. Students choose this if they think $Kr^{3+}$ loses 4s electrons first in a confusing way or miscounts its p electrons, but it is $4p^3$ just like N.
options.C: Incorrect. This would mean only 2 and 3 are correct. Students choose this if they forget that $Cl^+$ loses a p electron to become $3p^4$, and wrongly think it still has 1 unpaired like Cl.
options.D: Incorrect. This would mean only 1 is correct. Students choose this if they mishandle the unusual ions $Ga^-$ and $Kr^{3+}$ and assume negative ions or 4th period ions cannot match simple 2nd period counts.
